title: Bumble shares soar after report dating firm in $1bn takeover talks
content: Shares in dating app company Bumble soared by almost 50% on Monday after a report that it is in advanced talks to be bought for around $1bn (£757m). Technology holding company Ithaca could announce a deal to buy the Texas-based firm as early as this week, according to the Wall Street Journal. The jump in Bumble's shares pushed its stock market valuation to over $580m but that is still far below a peak of more than $14bn it reached after listing on the Nasdaq in 2021 . Bumble is one of the world's most downloaded dating apps, operating in a crowded market where growth has slowed. The BBC has contacted Bumble and Ithaca for comment. Bumble was launched in 2014 by Whitney Wolfe Herd, who was also a co-founder of dating app giant Tinder. Wolfe Herd built Bumble's brand around a distinctive feature that only allowed women to initiate conversations with matches. It recently abandoned that rule , prompting debate among users over whether the app had lost what set it apart from rivals. "Today, our community is asking for more flexibility, less pressure, and more opportunities to create real, meaningful connections and that is what this new experience provides," Wolfe Herd said in August. Dating apps like Bumble have come under pressure in recent years as some younger users have grown disillusioned with browsing for dates. Bumble said in 2025 that it would cut almost a third of its workforce as the industry grappled with what Wolfe Herd described as an "inflection point" in online dating. Investments in other dating companies have also soured as apps have struggled to convince users to pay for their services. Match Group - which owns apps including Tinder, OkCupid and Hinge - has also seen its shares fall sharply from their peak in 2021. According a report by media watchdog Ofcom in 2025, adults in the UK were spending less time on dating apps compared to three years earlier. Some single people are instead turning to board game get-togethers , book clubs and other group activities in the hope of finding a partner. The long-running claim alleges Grindr breached UK privacy laws by sharing data with third parties. Detectives are investigating two robberies and one attempted robbery. Users say dedicated platforms help them avoid discrimination and find meaningful relationships. The dating app's boss says the move is in response to a successful trial and a change in what users want. From women making the first move to shifting relationship dynamics, Love Island has become a window into Britain's evolving dating culture Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Qantas flight grounded after bedbug outbreak
content: A Qantas flight from Italy to Australia was cancelled on Saturday, after an outbreak of bedbugs on the plane. During the previous flight on Friday - a nearly 17-hour journey from Perth to Rome - some passengers had complained that they were being bitten by bugs, according to the Sydney Morning Herald. They were reportedly given antihistamines to help ease the itch of the bites, but supplies ran out. The Boeing 787 Dreamliner had to be grounded for "a deep clean", a Qantas spokesperson told the BBC. "We sincerely apologise to customers for the cancellation of Saturday's Rome to Perth service, which allowed our engineers and maintenance teams to carry out a deep clean of the aircraft after an issue was identified on a small number of economy seats," the spokesperson said. All affected customers were provided with accommodation and were rebooked on alternative flights within 48 hours of their original departure, the carrier said. Bedbugs are small, wingless parasites that can live on clothes, furniture and bedding. Their bites can be itchy but they do not usually cause more serious health problems, the NHS website says . But they can be difficult and expensive to get rid of. Treatment includes washing all bedding, clothing, and household materials like curtains on a hot wash and tumble dry, or they can be put in plastic bags in a freezer for three or four days. Bedbugs causing travel chaos is not unusual - less than two weeks ago, several Southeastern train services in England were cancelled after drivers discovered the creepy-crawlies in their cabs. In 2017, British Airways apologised to a family travelling from Vancouver to London, after they were left covered in bug bites from an overnight flight. And Turkish Airlines faced with a PR nightmare last year after the New York Times reported of several instances of bedbug infestations on its planes - and allegations at the time that the airline did nothing about it. Oxford's new traffic trial is being blamed for long delays around the city's station area. Meeting travellers' expectations could be challenging, experts warn. A rail-replacement bus has been in place for services to Redcar for two years due to the closure. Brittany Ferries' Barfleur has been sailing between Poole and Normandy for more than 30 years. Guernsey finishes ahead of Jersey and behind only the Isles of Scilly in the Condé Nast awards. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. The BBC is not responsible for the content of external sites. title: Boardroom feud tests trusted Indian business empire
content: Before dawn breaks over Mumbai, Mansi Kadam begins preparing vada pav, a savoury snack synonymous with the western Indian city, for the day's customers. One ingredient is non-negotiable: Tata salt. When asked whether she would ever consider switching brands, her reply is a reminder of an old Hindi ad jingle, "If it's salt, it has to be Tata." She knows little about the developments unfolding in the boardroom of the Tata group, one of India's oldest and most influential business empires that makes everything from salt to software. But her instinctive loyalty points to a question confronting the group: Can one of India's most trusted brands remain insulated from a public battle over power, governance and control? A recent public disagreement between the board of Tata Sons, the holding company of the Tata group and Tata Trusts, its principal shareholder, has put a spotlight on the conglomerate. At the centre of the dispute are two issues - the proposed public listing of Tata Sons and the reappointment of chairman N Chandrasekaran . Most of the Tata Sons board, including its biggest minority shareholder SP Group, supported the decisions. But Noel Tata, chairman of majority shareholder Tata Trusts, has opposed both resolutions. He maintains that a public listing would dilute the group's philanthropic ethos and is likely to get both decisions overturned at its annual general meeting. "When we say this is a governance crisis, it's a misalignment of interests between the board [of Tata Sons] and the shareholders [Tata Trusts]," Shriram Subramanian, head of independent corporate governance firm InGovern Research, told the BBC. While he does not expect the brand's image to be affected immediately, he flags concerns over the leadership's ability to navigate the challenges. Disagreements within the Tata Group have been simmering since the death of former chairman Ratan Tata - Noel Tata's half-brother who designated him successor after his death - in 2024. For many Indians, Ratan Tata's philanthropy and leadership had become inseparable from the brand. His death triggered widespread mourning and experts say it left a leadership void in the group's image with the public. The Tata group has topped India's most valuable brand list by valuation consultancy Brand Finance since 2018, according to the group's website. Tata Sons, the business entity, is described by the group as the "fastener keeping the many disparate elements of the whole together". Tata Trusts, which represents seven philanthropic trusts that own the majority stake in the group, is widely regarded as its moral compass, guiding the businesses on social impact and philanthropy. For many Indians, both the entities together make up what most companies cannot buy - trust. Now with these entities in rival corners, that is coming under strain. "Once upon a time, there was a unified audience which said the Tatas are good people with good governance. Today, the opinion is divided," said Harish Bijoor, business and brand strategy consultant. While most consumers appear unfazed, the dispute has polarised other stakeholders including business partners, investors and employees. Some view it as corporate power politics, others as a genuine governance debate, but few agree on which side is right, Bijoor said. "This conflict has brought the Tatas into conversations everywhere, which is not good as they have always liked to be out of it," he says. The group has been traditionally preferred being low profile about philanthropy and conflict resolution. The Tata group did not respond to BBC's email with detailed questions. Founded by Jamsetji Tata in 1868, the Tata group expanded under JRD Tata who transformed it into a professionally managed conglomerate. Ratan Tata drove its global ambitions through acquisitions. Tata group, which has a combined market value of more than $260bn (£195.6bn) and employs hundreds of thousands of people in more than 100 countries, is not new to controversies. The conglomerate has faced protests over industrial projects, scrutiny of its Indian telecom business during a spectrum allocation controversy, a high-profile dispute with Japan's Docomo and, more recently, questions over Air India's performance . Some of its business decisions have also drawn attention, particularly Tata Steel's troubled Corus acquisition, though other overseas bets such as Tetley and Jaguar Land Rover were successful and helped expand the group's global footprint. Its biggest controversy was in 2016 when the Tata Sons board abruptly removed Cyrus Mistry as chairman and brought back Ratan Tata as interim head. Mistry, heir to the SP Group, was chosen by a team led by Ratan Tata himself. It led to a long battle which ended in 2021 with the Supreme Court ruling in the Tatas' favour. Last month, journalist Sucheta Dalal wrote in her column for Moneylife magazine that the Tata group has "weathered serious governance storms" and enjoys "special privileges available to no other business group [referring to a tax exemption granted to Tata Trusts for holding shares in Tata Sons]" because of a reputation built over decades. Most Tata watchers agree. In an email interview, Morgen Witzel, a fellow at Exeter Centre of Leadership who wrote a book on the brand in 2010, cited several examples on the group's connection with people. At Jamshedpur in Jharkhand state, where the group set up India's first integrated steel plant and an industrial city, it provides healthcare and education to people in hundreds of villages. Watchmaker Titan supports employees who want to leave and start their own businesses. Tata Motors at Pune has supported thousands of female entrepreneurs, he points out. "It is the concatenation of all of these things that builds trust because people see that, by and large, Tata is there to serve their needs rather than just take their money," Witzel said. But while the group has weathered other storms, this time, the divide is within. The boardroom tussle has increasingly spilled into the public domain, with Tata Sons and Trusts clashing through legal notices and conflicting statements. Venu Srinivasan, vice-chairman of Tata Trusts and a nominee director on Tata Sons' board, has sought a probe into alleged governance lapses at some trusts. The trusts deny the lapses. Noel Tata has made two proposals to avoid listing the company. First, that the Tata Sons board buy back a portion of SP Group's minority stake as a "fair and equitable solution" to the latter's demand to monetise their stake. Secondly, restructure Tata Sons by merging with itself two businesses which would change the way it is classified by India's central bank, helping the group potentially avoid a listing. It is not clear whether he can pull this off, given that unlike Rata Tata, he had not consolidated power yet. "Ratan Tata's larger-than-life image is, to some extent, the reason behind the current conflict. Everyone was deferential towards him and his successor was known only after his death through his will," says Subramanian. Had Ratan Tata overseen the succession himself, the transition would have been smoother, he says. Brand expert Bijoor calls for the Tata group to put together a "white paper" on how the conflict plays out in the end. "They stood for transparency, and they must never shed that." How the influential group manages these tensions may offer a glimpse into its future. The outcome will be watched closely across corporate India, where Tata's governance and business practices have long been regarded as a benchmark. "Not a single drop has come through our taps for the last three months," a local tells the BBC. JJ Savani says his life changed when a mystery donor paid for him to do a barbering course. A desperate junta is in a war of attrition against ethnic militias and civilian resistance. Former students launched their own investigation, spending years collecting evidence and testimonies from others who say they were abused by the headteacher. Several trains to Delhi have been cancelled and dozens of metro stations are shut to stop protesters from gathering. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: I earn £120,000 a year making social media videos go viral
content: Eknoor Singh says he only needs his mobile phone and a decent internet connection to earn more than £120,000 a year. The 22-year-old Londoner is a professional "clipper". He is paid by clients to make short, vertical videos for social media, in the hope of them going viral. "The more views a clip gets, the more money I make," he says. The way it typically works is that the client - who could be anyone from a clothing brand to a record label, movie studio, podcaster or influencer - has a longer video that the clipper watches first. He or she then makes 30 to 60-second clips of what they consider to be the best bit or bits, and uploads them to Instagram, YouTube, TikTok or other platforms. The idea is that the clippers, who are typically aged from 16 to 25, will have a better understanding of what will connect with that demographic, and get the short videos as many views as possible. With clippers able to earn up to $3 (£2.30) per 1,000 views across platforms, it can be very lucrative if a particular clip does take off. Singh says he got hooked on clipping last year when he made $300 from posting a short video of popstar Dua Lipa on Instagram. "I was like, 'OK, this is a lot of money for simply posting a video.' I instantly knew how lucrative it could be." Now he says he is earning "at least £10,000 a month". He adds that he looks for clips that are funny, quick to watch and engaging, such as a short video he made in May of Sabrina Carpenter's reaction to having the tails of her dress stepped on at the Met Gala in New York. Singh did not reveal who the client was. For 24-year-old clipper Ethan Weems from Wichita, Kansas, it's a lucrative side hustle to his other video-making work. He says he makes "at least $1,000 a month" from clipping. He does this by making short videos for YouTuber and podcaster Caleb Hammer, who is best known for hosting a show called Financial Audit, which analyses the personal finances of his guests. Weems says clipping helps him make a living from home – giving him more time to spend with his wife and one-year-old son. "I don't want that typical nine-to-five job where I have to go into an office every day," he says. Yet while some clippers can make good money, social media consultant Lia Haberman cautions that there are very few of them. "It mirrors the creator economy more broadly. The vast majority make little to nothing," she says. Meanwhile, streaming industry analyst Devin Nash says it's easy to underestimate the time required to make clipping a success. He warns that successful clippers must "watch hours and hours of content, and they just live in that world". Connecting clippers with their prospective clients are a number of intermediary websites, where available video jobs are listed. These range from pages on general online forums such as Reddit and Discord, to dedicated clipping sites such as Clipping Culture, Vyro, Whop and Kick. The latter websites take a fee from the companies wanting the work done. Clipping Culture lists clients including Capital Records, Universal Music Group and HBO Max. For firms such as these, hiring a teenager or 20-something working from his or her bedroom is far cheaper than paying for traditional adverts on social media, and likely to be more effective in terms of getting eyeballs. That's the experience of Boxabl, a Las Vegas-based firm that makes modular homes. "I think we've done probably a billion views [of clips] so far," says founder Galiano Tiramani, who features in many of the company's videos. In the UK, Jimmy McLoughlin, a former Downing Street adviser and now host of the Jimmy's Jobs of the Future podcast, has also embraced clips. "The clips are almost like trailers for the main events," he says. For instance, a recent podcast with Prime Minister Andy Burnham "had close to 50,000 long plays, but in terms of clips, it's done millions". Evan Stanfield, the founder and boss of Clipping Culture, is himself just 21. He set up the business last year after dropping out of the University of Kansas. Stanfield says that the website connects brands to more than 340,000 clippers from all over the world. He has a simple theory for the popularity of short videos: "People's attention spans are getting shorter and shorter." He adds that making the clips is a young person's game because "they're most of the consumers of short-form videos". Back in London, Eknoor Singh says he is "kind of clipping non-stop", wherever he is. "I could be anywhere. I could go on holiday and make money." The jump pushed Bumble's stock market valuation to more than $580m but that is still far below their peak of more than $14bn. Mum and son team Choo and Chin Taylor have accumulated three million followers on social media. Firmus said it had made the decision due to "recent market volatility and prevailing market conditions". Solar tiles were touted as an attractive alternative to solar panels - why have they not taken off? Sun Yuanyuan was seemingly pictured on the back of another person's bike during part of the Berlin Marathon. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: I lost my hair to MS treatment - now my wigs are worn by Naomi Campbell and Serena Williams
content: When Antonia Okonma Shittu was told she had multiple sclerosis (MS) and would be using a wheelchair within the year, she was in denial. The 26-year-old, who was in between acting jobs and working in a call centre, said the diagnosis was a "massive turning point" in her life. "It does really make you think about what you want to do in life," she said. She looked back to what she enjoyed doing as a child - styling hair - and decided to use the shock of the diagnosis to spur her on to turn her passion into a business. Antonia, who grew up on a council estate in west London, bought two wigs and went door to door selling them from the boot of her car. Almost two decades later, she is now a multi-million-pound brand owner, with high-profile clients including tennis icon Serena Williams, model Naomi Campbell and actress Niecey Nash. She even won a Black British Business Award last week . Antonia, now 44, still struggles with her health, having also received diagnoses of Graves' disease - an autoimmune condition - and heart failure, but hopes her experience running a hair empire while fitting in hospital appointments can inspire other women. Antonia says she saw a gap in the market when she was surrounded by "terrible" wigs while working in TV and film, including in the ITV series Bad Girls two decades ago. "Women wanted natural-looking wigs and they just weren't available. They looked like helmets!" Antonia set up a Facebook page and began advertising on Gumtree. "I had very limited resources. I didn't have any investors behind me. I come from very humble beginnings." Her experience dealing with MS has helped her success, she says. Antonia lost her hair when she underwent chemotherapy following a bone marrow transplant, so she knows what it is like to be "completely bald". This made her relate more deeply to her customers, she explains, as she understands the loss of control some women feel when they lose their hair. "I didn't feel like myself," she says, "but being able to put on a wig that looks something close to how your hair was, or the look you used to have, it's as though you can feel like yourself again." When she sees a woman put a wig on and her "whole face lights up", it can be "very, very rewarding". "When we feel good about ourselves...we're more confident, we can achieve more. I felt like I was changing the world, one person at a time." While Antonia's business, A-List Lace Hair, has grown from strength to strength, with salons in London and New York, she has been dealing with the impact of her health conditions. She struggles with fatigue due to her MS and uses a wheelchair, but says this has not stopped her success. Instead, it has simply changed the way she has run her business. "I used to feel that being a good entrepreneur was being able to do as much as I can myself," Antonia said. "Due to my health challenges, there are days where I literally can't feel my legs, they feel like jelly, there's days where I'm completely exhausted after sleeping, I wake up completely shattered." This has forced her to "trust other people and gain strength in building a team". As a woman in business, being in a wheelchair can sometimes make Antonia feel "smaller" as people often have to look down at her at industry events. "People are often surprised when I start speaking about my business, as though they're thinking 'how have you accomplished all of this in a wheelchair?'" Antonia, who has three young children, says that being underestimated can be a good thing, and she wants to remain open about her health to inspire other women. She says she used to feel "weak" because of her disability, but now feels she has gained "so much strength" from sharing her experience online. Asked what she would say to another woman who may fear her age, disability or health could get in the way of success, she says: "I would encourage them to just start." "You might not have control over your health, you might not know what tomorrow is going to bring, and you might not have all the resources. But start with what you do have, and let's see what could happen next." Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. The BBC is not responsible for the content of external sites. title: Heating oil customers face tough winter despite shake-up promise
content: Heating oil customers facing soaring bills have been promised better regulation of the sector by the government. Ministers say they will tighten up rules, promote competition and give customers clearer compensation routes if things go wrong. Minimum order levels, set for some customers, will be reviewed. With prices close to having doubled in the past year, some campaigners have called for heating oil customers to benefit from the same cap as regular, variable gas and electricity tariffs in England, Scotland and Wales. But there is no sign of the government proposing such a change, nor when the stricter rules will take effect. Ministers said they would work with industry to "develop a regulatory regime for the heating oil market, protecting consumers and promoting competition". In the meantime, oil users have been offered discounts on heat pumps, a code of practice is in place, and industry practices setting minimum order volumes at 500 litres for some consumers will be reviewed. Domestic tanks typically hold between 1,000 and 2,000 litres. The government said this had left some people having to pay for more heating oil than they might need. Prices have soared since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran. In March, the government announced a support package worth £53m for low-income families who use heating oil. The funding is distributed by local authorities, which set their own criteria for eligibility. A subsequent inquiry by the UK's competition watchdog, the Competition and Markets Authority, found that 1,700 households were forced to "re-order at significantly higher prices or go without fuel" after the war broke out, costing them up to £350. But those whose orders were cancelled and prices raised were told they were entitled to compensation. The government has now announced it will accept the CMA's recommendation to strengthen regulation in the sector. Energy minister Polly Billington said: "Thousands of heating oil customers felt they had nowhere to turn when they paid the price of rising oil and gas costs earlier this year. "We won't accept that. Energy is an essential good and people should not have to think twice about whether they're protected in the market. That's why we will reform the sector." Nick, a heating oil customer from West Suffolk, told the BBC's Your Voice that "off-grid households remain a major policy blind spot" for the government. "Any protection from UK government for domestic heating oil users will be very welcome, providing this is for all domestic heating oil users," the 28-year-old said. He rents a three-bedroom home with his partner. He said they had seen prices more than double in a year, to quotes of 111p per litre. "Heating my home is now no longer another household bill, but almost an investment," he said. He called on tax cuts for customers, or the extension of the price cap to heating oil - a demand also made by charity National Energy Action. Tim Buckman, chief executive of price comparison site Boiler Juice, told the BBC he wants stronger protections for consumers but the main problem was that heating oil is twice as expensive as it was before the war. "Just putting regulation in place is not going to reduce the price for customers. What we would like to see is the VAT off heating oil or targeting that specifically." Some 1.5 million households depend on heating oil, but they do not have the same consumer protections as electricity and gas customers. However, energy regulator Ofgem, which sets the cap for standard variable tariffs, only covers England, Wales and Scotland. Most heating oil customers are in Northern Ireland, where 60% of households rely on it, but where regulation is separate. It is likely Ofgem will regulate heating oil in England, Scotland and Wales, and the UK government said it would "engage with the Northern Ireland Executive as they consider these recommendations in parallel". The education minister has warned it would immediately cost his department £20m a year at a time when it is already struggling to balance its budget. The rural communities vulnerable to heating oil prices rises as the weather gets colder. Cancer charity Daft as a Brush and Teesside Minibus Hire say they are struggling with pump prices. Ukraine's president sharply criticised the move, calling it an "investment in war that must be ended, not prolonged". The price of fuel has soared as the cost of living emerges as a key issue for millions of Americans. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved.
